figures.alt: Illustration of a Michigan field in early morning with the Sun low behind a row of trees, and long tree shadows stretching across the grass toward the viewer.
figures.caption: When the Sun is low, shadows are long and point away from the Sun.

figures.alt: Illustration of the Milky Way and many stars over a dark lakeshore with pine trees in silhouette.
figures.caption: The Milky Way is our galaxy, seen as a faint band of many stars. The night sky changes by season because Earth orbits the Sun.

figures.alt: Illustration of a pencil stuck in clay on white paper in strong sunlight, with its long shadow falling across the paper, a few chalk marks along the shadow, and a ruler beside the paper.
figures.caption: The shadow-clock kit: mark the tip of the shadow at different times and see how its length and direction change.

figures.alt: Interactive: a slider moves a ball around a picture of Earth and a button drops it. The arrow always points to the center of Earth.
figures.caption: Move around the globe and drop the ball from anywhere: it always falls toward the center of Earth.

figures.alt: Interactive: a slider sets the time of day from 8:30 am to 3:30 pm and shows the shadow of a 10 centimeter stick in a top view, with its length and direction.
figures.caption: Slide the time of day and watch the shadow change length and direction while the Sun moves.

figures.alt: Bar graph of shadow length of a 10 cm (about 4 inch) stick with direction. 8:30 am: 34 cm (about 13 inches), west. 10:00 am: 20 cm (about 8 inches), northwest. 12:00 pm: 9 cm (about 3.5 inches), north. 2:00 pm: 18 cm (about 7 inches), northeast. 3:30 pm: 30 cm (about 1 foot), east. Shortest at noon.
figures.caption: Shadow of a 10 cm (about 4 inches) stick on a sunny day in about March or September. The shadow is shortest at noon (9 cm, about 3.5 inches, pointing north) and long in the morning and afternoon (34 cm, about 13 inches, at 8:30 am). It points west in the morning and east in the afternoon, away from the Sun.
